review_text_raw:
A story about an idiot surrounded by other idiots who sound like idiots.

At no point was there any reason to sympathize with Anna and her lifetime of bad decisions that got her into this mess. She's like the stereotypical white person in a horror movie whose phone suddenly goes to static and runs out of gas in the middle of the night in front of an obviously haunted house and says "I should investigate this immediately, and by myself!". Her dumbass ex, her dumbass new lover, her dumbass "best friend", all of whom supposedly want to help her yet they somehow form the main obstacles to doing so, especially the "best friend" who is basically a secondary antagonist for all the help she is. Aside from bit players like the completely unconvincing cop. I thought the cop was lying about being a cop and that that was important as first, but nope, just terrible voice acting, we're supposed to believe that's what cops sound like. Though he's not as bad as the villain revealed at the end, who sounds like a 13 year old boy who got his big brother to install voice changing software for him because he thinks it'll make him sound badass on voice chat while playing Halo. It's that bad. Was it supposed to be intimidating? Was it supposed to be a shocking reveal? It wasn't, just the annoying end to a nonsensical story about thoroughly unsympathetic idiots. Nothing about this is redeemable, this was a waste of a Humble Bundle pick. And they had the nerve to release a sequel? Why, because they can churn out terrible games like this once a week? I hope it at least has an "everyone dies" ending, because after meeting all of these characters, I honestly don't want any of them to live, it would be better for society for every one of them to go away.

I really don't like Steam's binary review system. I feel like "some" people would like this game... but to me it's suffering the following:

[list]
[*]Imbalance between (unintended?) camp and "horror" (mostly to do with a couple V/O performances)
[*]EXTREME over-reliance on jump-scares (which takes away from the investigation/mystery aspect)
[*]Some rough writing here and there
[*]Some "simulated choice" options (i.e. you HAVE to say things even if you wouldn't want to or it wouldn't make sense for your character to)
[*]Some REALLY obscure puzzles that have had to be answered by the developers themselves

All-in-all it's not a "bad" game... but it's a great "idea" with some execution misses.

That being said, if you love jump-scares and some weird screwed up imagery with "INTENSE" sound effects, etc. then you might dig this. If I were to arm-chair develop this, I would have held back on some of the jump scares to make them more effective than just annyoing, and leaned more into the "missing person investigation" aspect of things vs. bringing in the [spoiler]supernatural[/spoiler] elements so quickly. 

I think the overall presentation and mechanics are solid... none of my critiques of this game are "budget-related," but more about writing/pacing/etc. 

I'm gonna give this a "no" but with a big caveat, that I wouldn't recommend it to MOST people... I really think something special and unique is buried under the surface of this game, but I think maybe the development team just got a little to shy of the story itself and decided to overload it with trope-y jumpscare image-horror to cover it up a bit. 

I know these games are made by real people, and I empathize with the team behind this and hope they know that my "negative" review comes with a healthy does of optimisim that they have something great in them and look forward to their next go of it!

Playable, but not to my tastes.

Simulacra is a simple investigative game that requires patience not for the investigation itself, but for its unnatural writing (very clearly non-native English) and its amateurish acted scenes. Jokes dropped like lead balloons, tension dissipated, and what should have been an exciting climax was simply uncomfortable.

The puzzles themselves were relatively entertaining - flicking between apps to piece together information - but the game's "OS" seemed almost incapable of multitasking, and switching between tabs would typically lose form entry data, making the process far more tedious than it should have been.

The game encourages the player to play through multiple times (with a fast-dialogue option after completion), but one playthrough felt like a slog, so I'm unlikely to sit through it again. If you happen to have it in your Steam library, give it a shot, but don't get your hopes too high.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a found phone horror game. The premise of the game is that you (the unknown, nameless protagonist – but presumably *you*, the actual player) found a phone out on your front porch that belongs to a woman named Anna. There’s something off about the phone, though; it keeps glitching out, a number of the files on it are messed up, there’s some creepypasta-esque flashes of the screen changing to horrifying images – and of course it quickly becomes evident from the frantic messages you get from her boyfriend that Anna has gone missing.

The game’s basic premise is exploring Anna’s phone. You decrypt some images and text messages via very simple minigames, but most of it is a choices-matter narrative, as you interact with not only Anna’s boyfriend, but a funny guy named Taylor on Spark (a dating/hookup app that *totally* isn’t Tinder) who had been flirting with Anna, as well as messages from Ashley, Anna’s best friend. You browse a few in-game websites, make a few phone calls from phone numbers you find on them and hidden in various images, and gradually unravel the mystery of what happened to Anna over the course of the game.

This is something of a hybrid of a simple puzzle game and Telltale’s sort of narrative storytelling, where you have a list of dialogue choices and they influence how other characters react to you. There is actually a branching narrative – the choices you make actually influence which endings you can access as you try to save Anna, only to discover that things aren’t so easy, and how you treat the characters affects how they interact with you. If you’re a jerk to someone, they won’t trust you and will be a jerk back; if you’re nice to them, they’ll be more trusting. But at the same time, you can lie about who you are to various people in the game, and while sometimes they’ll figure it out, other times you’ll slot right in as a trusted person and be able to get what you need out of them.

Indeed, pretense is a major theme of the game – people aren’t quite who they present themselves to be online, and the fronts they put up often don’t match who they are (or, indeed, who they perceive themselves to be). Is Anna’s boyfriend really still together with her, or did they break up, and is he stalking her? There’s a bunch of sexual predators on Spark – is Taylor one of them? Does Ashley have ulterior motives in her friendship with Anna?

I’d like to say that the biggest flaw with this game is that the resolution is, perhaps, a bit on the nose. While I approve of this new age of horror, and coming up with a new spooky villain, I also didn’t feel like it did a good enough job of reinforcing the manipulation angle of social media, instead simply resorting to outright mind control, which was a lost opportunity.

However, I think the actual largest flaw with this game is that it is just okay. It is a clever idea, and there are some fun conceits in there, but I have to say at the end I was left feeling just lukewarm about it. When I play a game, or finish a game, I want a sense of satisfaction. But this was just sort of an experience I had. It wasn’t bad, but it wasn’t particularly excellent, either.

If you’ve never played a game like this before, and somehow got this for free or as part of a bundle, it’d be worth a spin to just try out something new. But at the same time, I’m left feeling like it’s hard to recommend that someone go out of their way to experience it, and when I recommend something, I want to actually be able to say to someone “Yes, you should go play this game.”

I wasn’t left with that feeling here, as while it is overall decent, it is all just a little bit flat, and the jump scares don’t manage to really carry the horror of the game very well.

review_text_raw:
I really love this game genre, but this specific game wasn't very good in my opinion, for the following reasons:
- Inconsistent plot. The game just makes use of random horror movie tropes, without them making sense in the story.
- Very cringey characters (both due to the bad writing and to the bad acting), ESPECIALLY the two most important characters in the game: the girl you're supposed to find and the ultimate bad guy. That's a real problem, because it makes it very hard to emphatize with the person you're supposed to save, as well as to take the bad guy seriously.
- Random jumpscares make this game feel pretty shallow.
- Very, very often, the choices that are proposed to you seem forced. Basically, you can feel that the game WANTS the story to progress in a specific direction, and doesn't allow you to very simply avoid issues by being reasonable. For example, at some point, you can either tell a very dangerous lie or tell the truth. But if you tell the truth, at no point does the game allow to explain yourself, and therefore the person you told the truth to just reacts badly for no reason. In real life it would have been easy to avoid that issue, but the game doesn't want that. Hence, choices aren't well made, and overall it doesn't feel like you're really making story progress - it actually more feels like you're following the story where it wants you to go.

Still, there also are some good things:
- The phone interface looks pretty realistic, which is at least one immersive thing
- One playthrough is reasonably long (about 4 hours for the first one), especially since the game is very cheap, and there apparently are four different endings. 
- One or two moments in the story were actually pretty interesting, even though they didn't make sense in the grand scheme of things

Overall, I advice against buying this game, as there are many better ones in the same genre; I for example enjoyed Orwell much more, and both its mechanics and thematics are somewhat similar (without the horror movie aspect of it, which is good riddance honestly), but the writing is much better and realistic (and therefore more immersive as well !) and never made me cringe. Still, Simulacra is very cheap, so if you're okay with what I said above, go ahead.

I wanted to recommend this game. However, here I am. After playing for nearly five hours and being highly invested in what was going on, solving the games puzzles (as they are) and overall having dialogue options that I like to pick. I find that in the end the game became a big let down. It bothers me how much of a mood swing it ended up being for me.  

I wont spoil anything, of course. But above where I mention my choices feeling like that are what I'd pick? Really? In the end it's not a thing. The horror aspect of this game is great in the sense you have no idea what has happened to Anna. The game leaves you clues along the way that can lead you to theories. You feel great when you can take what the game shows you and thirty minutes later you get a sense of satisfaction knowing you were able to collect the clues correctly.  

Yet, in the end. It does not matter. To say I dislike the ending of this game and that is why I am giving this the red thumb is true. 5 hours of an adventure down the rabbit hole was not enough for me to wash the bad taste out of my mouth from my finale experience. 

Regardless, I look forward to what Kaigan Games does in the future. The world building for this game was good, until... well.. the end.

Sigh.

I want to be kind to this game and for the right person, I would still recommend it. But I don't think SIMULACRA quite pulls it all off. I like the social media sleuth type games (e.g. A Normal Lost Phone.) And the horror twist on this one isn't even that bad if you don't mind breaking the whole simulationist vibe of it.

But there's quality issues. Acting and voiceover ranges from straight-faced to hammy and cartoony and it's not really clear which flavor is intended. There's also *a lot* of spelling and grammar errors that kind of break the sense of immersion. And worst of all, advancing the plot in many cases requires taking actions that the player might have a very good reason not to perform. If I suspect a character of harming the owner of this phone, why should I tell them everything I dig up from social media? Make it make sense.

review_text_raw:
The setting is a good idea. They are achieving a good ambiance with background noises that are really well mixed.
This is the only positive point in my experience.

The actual gameplay is very linear and highly undynamic. The investigation part of the game feels more like a checklist then actually trying to understand the persons involved. Why is that? The characters are all very plain and are represented in bad writing. They feel stereotypical to a point were I was only annoyed by their presence and had to figure out how to deal with their stupidity. Their language felt really unnatural and to top it off some video clips and voice calls to top it all off.
There were some interesting ideas, but in general the game feels rushed in really unpolished.
The options of dialogue were pretty straight forward, but as I already said it there are little subbranches to discover. The decision you make are making minor differences in the end scene. The achievements are less of a challenge, more a lure into replaying a game that has little to no replay value.

To finalize. Yes I agree that the concept is nice, but this game clearly lacks quality. Instead of trying to polish the game, they just move on the next. So Simulacra is left in a very bare bones state in the end.

4€ is a little price, I cant recommend it. If you have the money to spare I recommend games on Steam that are driven by passionate teams that are putting an continuous effort into improving their games. I highly recommend Terraria that is often available for 5€ on sale.

This game is a bit annoying. I kinda enjoyed my time with it but it's just not good.

On the plus side: it's got decent social media puzzles and a sufficiently creepy atmosphere, ... and that's about all it has going for it. On the minus side: The writing is terrible, the voice acting is not great, there are several cheap jump scares, and the story itself is awful.

Ooh, the story has multiple endings and I should play again? No thank you, once is enough. I can't see what the game could have to offer besides more weak dialogue and weird railroady decisions.

Spoilers, I guess, but I lost and got the worst ending because I didn't show enough trust in the sleazebag (who was specifically written as a sleazy dude) ALL THE WAY IN THE BEGINNING OF THE GAME. It always bunches my britches when a game does that: "Oh you didn't do a thing when you didn't have all the information yet and you couldn't make an informed decision about it? Sucks to be you, Anna's dead." Oh, and also Taylor, he's dead too. Just because I wouldn't send the sleazy dude a cute selfie of the missing girl and I wasn't sufficiently sad enough about him being caught with his pants down (literally, fuck, it's such a contrived story).

I feel like the game is less about saving Anna and more about how you're supposed to protect the feelings of the two douchebag brodudes. There's only one other recurring character, Anna's best friend, Ashley, who could have been of great help, but the story sidelines her almost immediately and only brings her back to intimate that she's secretly in love with Anna. Again, spoilers, but if you've read this far, I doubt you care. (edit: Reading someone else's review, I just learned that to get the absolute best ending, you have to catfish the best friend and reciprocate her feelings without Anna's consent or Ashley's knowledge. Cool game, bro!)

Anyway, don't bother with this game unless you really want a 5 hour puzzle game with a crappy story.

review_text_raw:
[b]Simulacra[/b] is a "found phone" game—a genre where players uncover clues after discovering a stranger's lost smartphone. While the concept has gained popularity in the last decade, games have experimented with faux interfaces mimicking imagined technology for years. I remember playing Mean Streets and the officially licensed X-Files game, both of which attempted something similar.

In Simulacra, you navigate the protagonist's phone within the game's tightly controlled framework, piecing together what happened to its owner. I was initially drawn to the game due to the resurgence of modern full-motion video (FMV) storytelling. Having enjoyed 2015's Her Story, I expected a similar experience. While Simulacra integrates FMV clips effectively, its "found phone" premise was far less compelling to me. I think I hit an audience mismatch—I’m simply not a fan of smartphones. Since I don't particularly enjoy using my own phone, the idea of rifling through someone else’s was unappealing. I played on my laptop and embarrassingly took about a third of the game to realize that it was undoubtedly designed to be played on a smartphone—duh.

The protagonist, Anna, feels like a generic twenty-something woman struggling with rocky relationships, an unfulfilling job, and repeated rejections in her academic and professional pursuits. [spoiler]She has a non-binary best friend, which the game seemingly frames as a revelation, but it’s so heavily telegraphed that it falls into cliché territory.[/spoiler] In fact, Anna herself is a walking cliché, as is the familiar "technology is evil" theme—an overused trope in uninspired sci-fi narratives. After seeing it so often, it no longer has much impact for me.

The game’s title did surprise me. Before playing, I had never encountered the terms "Simulacra" or "Simulacrum," which piqued my curiosity. Midway through, I looked up the meaning, wondering why a game about a woman's lost phone would have such a name. Ah, crap—spoilers.

As for gameplay, Simulacra offers little freedom. Players must follow rigidly scripted conversations in a precise order to unlock new options and clues. While there are minor choices in how you interact with Anna’s close friends, they ultimately boil down to a few dialogue changes that determine which of the five endings you get—most of which depend on choices made in the last 10% of the game. That said, I appreciated that I could make all the necessary connections without resorting to a guide or hints. That sense of progress and accomplishment is something lacking in other puzzle or adventure games.

Overall, Simulacra is predictable but not necessarily bad. The FMV clips are well-integrated, Wendy Van Horen Carneiro delivers a solid performance as the wronged damsel in distress, and the faux-phone interface is thoughtfully designed. I give it a [b]3 out of 5[/b]—though the game is clearly aimed at a different audience than me, so others may find it more engaging.

review_text_raw:
tl;dr if you want a phone snooping game that is better than this (harder puzzles, better writing) + touches on some of the same themes, and don't mind it being non-horror, try out [b]Another Lost Phone: Laura's Story[/b].

I really like the conceit of a fake computer or phone as the setting for a mystery game, which is why a friend recommended I play this. However, I can't say that I would do the same.

The writing is riddled with typos and unnatural grammatical errors. Like, a lot of these characters aren't even convincingly fluent English speakers. (Also the way their only Black character is written is. reductive.) But it does have its moments that feel natural and compelling.

The acting is... bad. They sound like they're reading off a teleprompter one word at a time, rather than speaking a sentence, and the emotional reactions are not convincing. Worst of the bunch is, unfortunately, one of the two guys whose voice you hear the most. [spoiler](By which I mean Greg.)[/spoiler]

The characterization is weird? IDK, you spend most of your time talking to various brands of Men Who Are Creepy To Women, and it keeps asking you to side with at least one of them. [spoiler]By the way, one of them is a registered sex offender. And somehow, that's not even the reason he's creepy![/spoiler] Even your interactions with the women in the cast are usually about various aforementioned creepy men. [spoiler]The closeted lesbian coming out to (she believes) the woman she has a crush on? That conversation fails the Bechdel test, even if you consider the player impersonating Anna to be a "named woman."[/spoiler] So even though it's supposed to be about Anna, it's more accurately about men fighting over a woman-shaped trophy called Anna.
It may seem like I'm kind of harping on this but that's only because so MUCH of their characterization is either behaving inappropriately towards women or being belligerent to people in general. There's not much to go on without that.

As for the narrative, it was... railroady. I didn't feel like I was finding secrets because even if I found out something a little early, one of the guys would just tell me to do it later. The highly telegraphed railroading in the intro was actually my favorite UI moment in the game, but that was a lot more artful than the clumsy dialogue trees that all lead to a single point.
I did think the big bad was interesting, especially the part about [spoiler]how "a strong individual would simulate a better [life]" rather than live fully in a suboptimal one[/spoiler]. Though I felt like that theme of [spoiler]the appearance being more meaningful than the substance[/spoiler], while present in some parts of the game, such as [spoiler]reporting a colleague for harassment being an issue because it could reflect poorly on the company, or the folder of pictures of random women that Taylor just Has, Apparently[/spoiler], was underutilized. Which is odd, because... that's from your villain monologue—you HAVE to establish those themes in the story up to that point.

There's just a lot that could have been considerably better than it was.

All the characters I interacted with were unlikeable, and I didn't like how the game forced melodrama between the two main dudes. It wasn't about figuring out Anna's inner demons or psychology, but about figuring out how to "handle" these guys so they would keep helping you. I can honestly say it combined all the crappiest parts of horror movie trailers, the worst creepypastas and a s****y jigsaw puzzle together in a terrible phone-shaped package that lasted for WAY too long. It's not going to get better.

Got this from the "Overwhelmingly Positive" Humble Bundle. How in the actual f*** is this game "Overwhelmingly Positive" ????? Kids review bomb awesome games on here all the time, and this managed to survive that for so long? I'm legitimately confused and concerned. Did this game get massive press in some media targeted specifically towards children, and somehow avoid literally everyone else? Did the people who hate it just not care enough to leave a review? Again, were on Steam, so how?????

On a particularly boring night, I played the entire damn thing. The first 5 minutes in I already knew it was going to be terrible, but stupidly I played on, hoping for something redeeming to happen to justify the positive reviews and my time wasted. That obviously didn't happen.

Bad writing, bad puzzles, atrocious "scares" (literally all jumps, flashing images and noises, and even then not a single f***ing one even managed a startled shutter from me, with volume annoyingly high), all set to an all-too-overplayed by now "hey, play this game on this device/OS/form of communication" gimmick that I'm frankly by now beyond tired of game developers using as a replacement for an interesting story/plot/writing (Stories Untold is the most recent game to do it RIGHT AFAIK). It was cool like the first 100 times maybe, but I'm over it.

I also want to point out, I don't think I have EVER seen good writing/plot in a game that has characters communicating through a messaging system, then has every character using terrible grammar, punctuation, etc. It bugs the hell out of me.
1.It's usually inconsistent. Some chatacters just spring in and out of it randomly.
2.We're not all 12. Some people actually care about that kind of stuff, so it doesn't make sense to have EVERYONE at some point talking like the slow, overly emotional kid in class.
3.It isn't 1995 anymore. It's one thing to have every character talk like that when they're using AOL Instant Messenger, but for chrissakes, you actually have to make an EFFORT to screw up grammar the way these characters do on a modern cellphone with autocorrect. Ugh.

The game has potential with its premise.
However, it handles it so, so poorly.
Tried all the endings and variation of the game.

The interface is crisp and the chat messages actually pretty good. Going through messages, characters are both flawed and likeable and the writing does text messaging very well, it doesn't feel too cringe nor too forced.

The thing is, going through someone's messages and all that already does what the game wants; think about what you're doing with someone's privacy. However, by the end of it, it will rub its "simulacra" psychological message in your face in the edgiest, most infantile way. I get it, its a black mirror, its such a smart and deep(TM) plot you have.

But the worst part of the game is the acting.
Upon playing, you will see a set of videos and some people (aka one character) will send you video messages. The thing is.
THE. ACTING. IS. MONSTROUSLY. CRINGE.
It is very, very, VERY bad acting. Not in the way that sometimes in a small game, you'll see a dev do a few lines and it feels a bit awkward, but it's serviceable. No. I have no idea who the actors are, but they feel like very, VERY bad amateur actors trying way too hard to be good actors, but also act like they think they are very good actors. One of the character is supposed to be to some extent a cringy kind of person, but it is not the character that is cringe, the way the actor playing the character is really cringe. I have no idea who the actors are, but it genuinely feel like the it's the dev who just hired his girl crush being like "You have a cute face you're gonna be a star in my game". It is just that tryhard cringy.

Now you think "Oh its a phone game so you'll mostly see text messaging". No, by the time you reach the second half, you'll be bombarded with video and they will be all as painful to watch as the next one. Which is a goddamn shame, because during my playthrough, the messaging back and forth with those characters felt good and compelling.

If you're curious about the game, really, just watch a playthrough online.

review_text_raw:
Sad to say that I had to refund this. The premise seemed solid based on the store page - trying to piece together clues to someone's disappearance when you only have their phone - and the general interface was well done, but that was about it. My first hour of playing this mostly consisted of:

[list]
[*] Listening to overdramatic, very slowly worded voice messages.
[*] Piecing together "corrupted" pictures and texts that had absolutely nothing to do with Anna's disappearance. 
[*] Wondering if a proofreader was ever used for this game. Most of the articles and texts gave me the impression that English isn't the developer's first language. While I have nothing against that, coming across awkward grammar really took the immersion out of a mostly text-based game.
[*] Sitting through consecutive rounds of text-vomit finger-pointing from Greg and Taylor. I truly detest people who text at a rate of 50 messages/min when a single sentence would have sufficed. I didn't think it could get any worse, but in came the relationship drama...
[*] An overall disconnect between the gameplay and the plot. A girl disappears with clear hints of some non-human entity behind it, so why am I wasting my time investigating the sorry backgrounds of two garden-variety losers?
[/list]

Maybe the game gets better beyond the 1.7-hour point, but I really didn't have the patience to sit through constant notifications from the Male MC Idiot Express while waiting for some actual horror story to happen. Honestly, I'd have been happier to just shut the damn phone off and actually set out to find Anna door to door. At least then the "investigation" would have felt more productive.

Not the worst but I am surprised at how highly rated this was.
I didn't find it overly scary beyond a few jump scares.  The most believable characters in the game are Anna and her friend, I enjoyed their realistic sideconversations more than most others in this game.  The other 2 main characters were overhammed to the point of ridiculousness which was very jarring altogether.

As I found certain conversations softlocked at random points until you hit some other arbitrary checkpoint which unlocked the rest of the thread.  Also some things were just not implemented well.  In what world is a job interview carried out over text?  And every phone call was completely one-sided which was so strange - I don't know why they didn't let you select responses like in the written conversations.
Speaking of dialogue, I didn't feel I had great freedom of choice in responding in conversations - I felt I was always fighting with what I was allowed to say.  And the ending fell rather flat, with a certain character taking a complete 180 degree change in attitude and outlook just so the ending could be tied off in a semi-neat bow.
I do have the second game in the series as I got it in a bundle, and the game wasn't so awful as to put me off trying it, so I will see if these devs have taken on board lessons learned and improved things in the second go round, but this game as it stands I would not recommend it.

Simulacra is an interactive horror movie displayed through an emulated mobile phone screen.  You've got someone else's phone and for some reason you're texting her boyfriend and watching spooky videos because something went wrong.  Spooky technology glitches! oooOOOoooo. 

I think FMV can be an excellent tool in storytelling and video game creation if used right.  Looking at games that worked, like Press X Not To Die and Mortal Kombat, you can see why.  Simulacra isn't one of the ones that works.  The story is below Blair Witch 4 kind of stuff, it's not gripping.  The bits where you're texting other people is badly written.  I understand the developers wanted to emulate a mobile phone, but looking at my 4K monitor being wasted displaying a 9:16 aspect ratio is just depressing.

There's better ways to tell a story than we can see in Simulacra.  For less money than they're asking for this you could rent any schlock horror film online and have a far better time, with better writing and acting, too.  If you did end up with this in the Humble Bundle and accidentally launched it, be aware the game crashes when you try to exit, and you have to go find the rogue process and kill it.
